name: Nanofat / fat grafting tear trough

card.summary: The patient's own fat, moved into under-eye hollows; longer-lasting in theory, with sparse tear-trough-specific trial data.
card.aka: Autologous fat transfer, lipofilling, periorbital fat grafting
card.note: Fat necrosis, reabsorption and contour irregularities are documented; embolic complications are described with autologous fat.

quick.overview:
Fat grafting takes fat from elsewhere on the body, usually by liposuction, processes it and injects it into areas that have lost volume. In the under-eye region it is used to soften hollows where the lower eyelid meets the cheek. Nanofat refers to fat that has been broken down into a finer emulsion, which proponents describe as useful for thin skin.

It is a surgical procedure rather than a product, and it is discussed in appearance communities as an alternative to hyaluronic acid filler because the material is the patient's own tissue. Published tear-trough-specific trials are scarce.
quick.mechanism: Fat is harvested, handled to preserve cell survival, and re-injected into the target area to add volume. Some of it is reabsorbed, and reports describe stem-cell-related regenerative effects as a rationale for finer preparations such as nanofat.
quick.risks: Reported risks include swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain, infection, lumps or contour irregularity, fat necrosis and variable reabsorption. Embolic complications, including rare vision loss, are described with injectable materials and have been linked more often to autologous fat than to hyaluronic acid.

lead: Fat grafting, also called autologous fat transfer or lipofilling, is a procedure in which fat taken from one part of the body is processed and injected into another to restore volume or improve contour.[1] Under the eyes it is used to fill the tear trough, the hollow groove where the lower eyelid meets the cheek, so that the transition from eyelid to cheek looks smoother, the shadowing is reduced and the face looks more rested and youthful.[2][3] Because the filler is the patient's own tissue, it is discussed in appearance communities as a longer-lasting alternative to hyaluronic acid filler, though how long it lasts varies from person to person.[14]

A 2024 review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery describes fat loss from specific facial fat compartments as a major contributor to the aged look and presents fat grafting as a way to restore that volume. It divides grafts by particle size into macrofat, microfat and nanofat: the first two mainly add volume and also improve skin quality, while nanofat, an emulsified preparation, has been reported to improve skin texture and pigmentation.[2] Nanofat was introduced by Tonnard and colleagues in 2013; it is made by mechanically emulsifying fat until it passes through fine filters, which leaves a fluid that can be injected into thin, superficial skin and that contains stromal cells and microvascular fragments rather than intact fat cells.[13][16]

Research specific to the tear trough is mostly small. Randomised and retrospective studies have compared nanofat with platelet-rich plasma for infraorbital dark circles, and a 2025 series of 183 patients combined transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty with percutaneous nanofat injection into the tear trough and reported high satisfaction at six months or more.[5][15] Reviews of nanofat in general state that standardised preparation protocols and guidelines have yet to be established.[4][16]
On looksmax.org, under-eye threads weigh topical products, filler and surgery against each other, with surgical fat grafting sitting at the surgical end of the options.[6]

chain: Fat harvested from the body and processed
Placed in the tear trough or as nanofat in thin under-eye skin
Hollow and shadow soften, skin may look smoother
angle.text: Fat grafting adds volume to the under-eye hollow, which reduces the shadowed step between lower lid and cheek. Nanofat is used in the thinnest skin and is reported to improve skin quality and pigmentation as well.

sections.h: Background: the tear trough and facial volume
paras: The tear trough is the groove running from the inner corner of the eye diagonally down and outward across the lower eyelid-cheek junction. Plastic surgery reviews attribute much of the aged or tired look of this area to loss of fat in specific facial compartments, which deepens the groove and casts shadow beneath the eye [2]. Modern facial rejuvenation therefore tends to restore deflated compartments rather than relying only on removal of skin, a shift Wikipedia's fat-transfer article associates with work on facial fat compartments by Rohrich and Pessa (2007) and structural fat grafting described by Sydney Coleman (2006) [1].

Options for the area span hyaluronic acid filler, fat grafting, platelet-rich plasma and lower-lid blepharoplasty, sometimes combined [7][8]. Fat grafting is used when the main concern is hollowing rather than excess tissue [2][7].

The procedure has three stages: harvesting fat, often by liposuction, processing it, and injecting it into the target area.[1] Sources describe minimizing handling and re-injecting promptly to preserve graft survival.[1] Harvest and preparation methods, including cannula size and filter cartridges, determine whether the result is macrofat, microfat or nanofat.[2]

Nanofat is produced by mechanically emulsifying fat until it passes through fine filters, giving a fluid that can be injected with very thin needles into superficial layers. A 2021 review describes it as a compact bundle of stromal cells with regenerative and tissue remodeling potential.[4]

Fat transfer to the face has a long history in reconstructive and cosmetic surgery, and Wikipedia's fat-transfer article cites Coleman's 2006 paper on structural fat grafting as more than a permanent filler and Rohrich and Pessa's 2007 work on facial fat compartments as shaping the modern approach to restoring deflated compartments.[1] Zuk and colleagues' identification of multipotent cells in human adipose tissue in 2001 and 2002 supplied the regenerative rationale that later led to cell-rich preparations.[1]

In 2013 Tonnard and colleagues described nanofat grafting in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, reporting basic research and early clinical use of an emulsified, filtered fat preparation for superficial skin rejuvenation.[13][16] Later variants include versions without the final filtration step, centrifuged preparations and a collagenase-assisted version.[16] A 2021 World Journal of Stem Cells review reports that the emulsification reduces mature fat cells by about 95 percent and leaves a stromal-cell-rich product with components of roughly 400 to 600 micrometres.[16]

Lower-eyelid surgery addresses fat protrusion, skin laxity and the eyelid-cheek contour, and adjunctive midface fat repositioning is sometimes used to smooth the transition between lid and cheek.[7] Fat grafting is an alternative or complement for patients whose main concern is hollowing rather than excess tissue.[2][7]

Besides facial volume restoration, fat grafting is used in other regions such as the breast, and a 2021 paper on periorbital fat grafting by Marten and Elyassnia is among the references on Wikipedia's fat-transfer page.[1]

A 2024 review explains that harvesting and preparation, including cannula size and filter cartridges, divide grafts by particle size and cell type into macrofat, microfat and nanofat. Macrofat and microfat provide volume and are also described as improving skin quality; nanofat has been reported to improve skin texture and pigmentation [2]. Wikipedia describes nanofat as very small grafts containing no intact adipose cells whose stem-cell content remains useful, and attributes part of fat grafting's regenerative potential to adipose-derived stem cells, which Zuk and colleagues identified in human adipose tissue in 2001 and 2002 [1].

Nanofat grafting was described in a 2013 Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery paper covering basic research and early clinical use [13]. A 2021 review describes adipose tissue as a 'stem cell depot' and nanofat as a compact bundle of stem cells reported to remodel the extracellular matrix, enhance angiogenesis and modulate immune response at the site of injury; it also covers preparation methods, delivery and ethical concerns [4]. Because nanofat is a fluid that passes through fine needles, it can be placed in thin superficial skin where larger particles risk lumpiness [2][4].

The 2021 review describes Tonnard's method in general terms: fat is harvested through a multiport cannula, rinsed, passed through a fine nylon filter, then emulsified by being moved repeatedly between two connected syringes and filtered again. The process is mechanical rather than enzymatic, which the authors say lowers cost, time and regulatory burden compared with enzymatic stromal vascular fraction.[16] Authors of the 2025 tear-trough series described emulsifying resected lower-eyelid fat between two syringes and injecting it into the tear trough in three layers with the patient sitting upright, using a mean of about 1.1 mL for both eyelids.[15]

A review comparing preparation types notes that nanofat acts mainly on skin rejuvenation while volume loss is usually addressed by macrofat or microfat.[2] Reported cell counts per gram of lipoaspirate are higher for mechanically prepared nanofat than for enzymatic stromal vascular fraction in one study cited by the 2021 review.[16]

Listed complications include swelling, bruising, hematoma, paresthesia or donor-site pain, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities and injury from cannulas.[1] Fat necrosis and reabsorption are recognized concerns; Wikipedia cites reabsorption of up to about 50 percent in breast augmentation.[1]

Separately, an overview of injectable fillers states that rare blindness and delayed skin necrosis can follow embolization of injected material, and that necrosis is more often linked to autologous fat than to hyaluronic acid.[8]

A 2024 review cites a series of 98 cases of filler-induced vision changes across facial sites in which autologous fat was implicated in 47.9 percent and hyaluronic acid in 23.5 percent; it notes blunt cannulas appear to lower vascular occlusion risk with filler.[14] The nanofat review recommends checking for blood reflux, slow low-pressure injection and blunt cannulas for facial grafting.[16] In the 2025 tear-trough series, no embolism was reported.[15] Regulators treat cell-containing fat products under minimal manipulation and homologous use rules, and the nanofat review says the status of stromal components is not fully clear.[16]

sections.h: Fat grafting compared with filler and fat repositioning
paras: A 2024 narrative review in the Journal of Personalized Medicine examined 20 mostly observational studies comparing fat repositioning with hyaluronic acid filler for tear troughs, without pooling data. It reports that fat repositioning aims at structural change that often lasts several years and that satisfaction is high in most series, while hyaluronic acid filler gives immediate results that typically last about 6 months to 2 years and has been reported with more than 75 percent satisfaction in many studies.[14]

The same review lists fat-repositioning complications such as edema, granulomas, numbness, dry eye, ectropion and scleral show, and filler complications such as bruising, swelling, irregularities, the Tyndall effect and migration. It suggests, as the authors' reading of the literature, that surgery suits significant hollowing or excess skin in patients who want durable results, and that filler suits milder deformity and a non-surgical option.[14]

Wikipedia's blepharoplasty article describes fat repositioning as redistributing orbital fat along the infraorbital rim to smooth the lid-cheek transition, and fat grafting as moving the patient's own fat to areas of volume loss around the eye.[3]

A 2023 single-blinded randomised comparative trial in Dermatologic Surgery compared platelet-rich plasma with autologous fat transfer using nanofat for infraorbital dark circles.[5] A 2024 randomised trial of stromal vascular fraction, PRP and a Q-switched laser added to nanofat-treated dark circles and wrinkles under the eyes was later retracted by its journal.[9]

The 2025 Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology series of 183 consecutive patients (366 lower eyelids, mean age 26.9, 95 percent female) at a Hangzhou hospital was a single-centre retrospective case series without a control group. Patients had lower-lid bags with little or no skin laxity and received transconjunctival removal of orbital fat, with the removed fat emulsified into nanofat and injected into the tear trough. Satisfaction was 96.6 percent, tear-trough depression and dark circles improved with blinded photographic grading, skin elasticity did not change significantly, and fat retention was not quantified. Reported events were bruising and swelling resolving in one to two weeks, increased fine wrinkles in 5.5 percent, transient bloodshot eyes in 2.7 percent, undercorrection in 2.7 percent, and smaller percentages of chemosis, bag recurrence and hollowness; no infection, hematoma or fat embolism was reported.[15]

Other nanofat trials have addressed acne scars, wound healing, burn wounds and breast-reduction scars rather than the tear trough.[10][11] A completed phase 2/3 registration (NCT01461785, n=25, started 2012) evaluated activated platelet-rich plasma in human autologous fat transfer, a related but different question.[12] The 2021 nanofat review lists dark circles, hollow eyes and malar bags among reported applications but gives no periorbital outcome data, and states that much evidence is preclinical or from small clinical studies.[16]

In under-eye discussions on looksmax.org, users describe hollowing and dark circles and often weigh topical 'lipofilling agents' such as Volufiline, fillers and surgery against each other; one user wrote that they had tried many things for the tear trough and dark circles 'short of fillers/surgery' [6]. Surgical fat grafting appears at the surgical end of those options [6].

timeline.event: Zuk and colleagues identify multipotent stem cells in human adipose tissue, later cited as part of fat grafting's regenerative rationale.[1]
Coleman's paper on structural fat grafting as more than a permanent filler.[1]
Rohrich and Pessa report on facial fat compartments, shaping compartment-based volume restoration.[1]
Tonnard and colleagues describe nanofat grafting in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.[13]
A World Journal of Stem Cells review surveys nanofat preparation methods and notes standardisation is lacking.[4][16]
Randomised trial compares PRP with nanofat fat transfer for infraorbital dark circles.[5]
Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery review distinguishes macrofat, microfat and nanofat; a Journal of Personalized Medicine review compares fat repositioning with HA filler for tear troughs.[2][14]
Retrospective series of 183 patients combines transconjunctival blepharoplasty with percutaneous nanofat in the tear trough.[15]

lore.intro: Under-eye fat grafting is discussed in appearance communities mainly as the surgical, longer-lasting end of the options for hollows and dark circles.[6]

claims.claim: Fat grafting gives a more permanent tear-trough fix than filler because it is your own tissue.
claims.believers: Proponents describe fat as longer-lasting and natural-looking compared with hyaluronic acid that dissolves over months.[14]
claims.experts: A 2024 review reports durable results in fat repositioning series but notes no study quantified duration precisely and that fat retention varies; reabsorption is documented.[14][1]

claims.claim: Nanofat improves skin quality and dark circles, not just volume.
claims.believers: Surgeons and proponents say nanofat's stromal cells remodel skin and can improve texture and pigmentation.[2][16]
claims.experts: Reviews report improvement in texture and pigmentation, while noting standardised protocols are lacking and much evidence is small or preclinical; a comparative RCT of PRP versus nanofat exists for dark circles.[2][16][5]

claims.claim: Nanofat's stem cells regenerate the under-eye area.
claims.believers: Reviews describe adipose tissue as a stem cell depot and nanofat as a compact bundle with remodelling potential.[4]
claims.experts: The same literature says the functional roles of nanofat components are not yet defined and that guidelines are needed.[16]

claims.claim: Topical lipofilling agents such as Volufiline can fill tear troughs like fat.
claims.believers: looksmax.org users ask about topical lipofilling agents for under-eye hollowing and nasolabial folds and discuss trying them before filler or surgery.[6]
claims.experts: No published trial of such topicals for the tear trough is cited in the sources reviewed here.[6]

claims.claim: Fat in the tear trough is hard to correct if it goes wrong.
claims.believers: Some surgeons and patients say misplaced fat is harder to remove than filler, which can be dissolved.[14]
claims.experts: The 2024 review notes hyaluronic acid effects are adjustable and shorter, and lists lumps and irregularities among fat-related complications.[14][1]

claims.claim: Injecting fat near the eye carries a risk of blindness.
claims.believers: Forum and clinic commentary treat embolic vision loss as a feared rare complication.[14]
claims.experts: A review cites 98 filler-related vision cases with autologous fat implicated in 47.9 percent and HA in 23.5 percent, and recommends blunt cannulas and careful technique.[14][16]
